Lessons.Title: Divide Decimals by Whole Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: share a FRACTIONAL decimal dividend into a positive whole number of equal groups, a different operation from whole÷small-decimal. The 2021 source connects shaded hundredths grids, whole-number division facts and verbal explanations before presenting less scaffolded decimal quotients.

Warm-up: shade 0.80 of one square in hundredths and partition the eighty equal pieces into four equal groups. Each receives 20 hundredths, or 0.20. Explain why splitting the selected amount into four groups is not the same as counting how many 0.04-sized pieces fit into a whole.

Activity 1 — exact equal shares: 0.72÷3 has seventy-two hundredths shared among three, yielding24 hundredths each, or0.24. The more delicate case 0.5÷2 requires renaming five tenths as50 hundredths before splitting, giving25 hundredths=0.25. Compare another 0.75÷5=0.15 and explain how 15 hundredths ×5 returns75 hundredths.

Activity 2 — connect whole-number facts: use 72÷3=24 to reason 7.2÷3=2.4 and0.72÷3=0.24; keep divisor three fixed while dividend changes place value. Calculate 0.7÷2=0.35 and0.45÷5=0.09 using hundredths. Learners compare a first-party area strip with multiplication-inverse explanations.

Assessment: exact decimals are appropriate numeric checks; equitable partition drawings, identifying the whole, interpreting the dividend/divisor, and partner revisions from the source require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Share a decimal dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: A decimal less than one can be shared into equal groups without changing the original whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rename tenths as hundredths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dividing a small count of tenths may be easier when expressed as hundredths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale a known whole quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: The relationship among72÷3,7.2÷3 and0.72÷3 depends on which fractional unit the dividend counts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Divide hundredths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find0.72÷3.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Arrange the72 equal pieces into three equal groups.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rename tenths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find0.5÷2.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Split50 into two equal groups of25.

WorkedExamples.Title: Another share
WorkedExamples.Question: Find0.75÷5 and0.7÷2.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Restore hundredth units to each quotient.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An equal-sharing task with0.5 as the amount shared and2 recipients is not2÷0.5.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the original amount and number of groups before selecting operation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Drop hundredth scale after dividing72 by3
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The resulting24 is a count of hundredths, not24 complete wholes.

SummaryPoints: Decimal÷whole divides a fractional amount into fewer equal shares.
Rename tenths as hundredths when fractional groups need finer units.
Source diagrams and partner explanations are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Divide Decimals by Decimals
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret how many TENTHS or HUNDREDTHS fit in a decimal dividend, including one with both a whole part and fractional part. The source deliberately uses the SAME hundredths-grid picture to compare1.6÷0.1 with160÷10, making choice of units and original whole central to understanding.

Warm-up: describe one complete hundredths square plus sixty further shaded cells. If the full square represents1, the shaded amount is1.60 and contains16 strips of ten hundredths (each0.1). The same 160 individual cells can instead be interpreted as an integer count and grouped into tens, producing160÷10=16, with the unit interpretation stated clearly.

Activity 1 — related interpretations: calculate1.8÷0.1=18 by counting ten tenths per whole and eight more tenths. Compare the whole-count equivalent 180÷10=18. Calculate1.35÷0.01=135 by counting one hundred hundredths from the whole and35 extra hundredths; the decimal dividend is not rounded to1.4 or treated as one whole only.

Activity 2 — contrast divisors: 0.5÷0.1=5 but0.5÷0.01=50, because a fixed half-whole can be cut into five tenths or fifty hundredths. Likewise0.02÷0.01=2 and1.53÷0.01=153. Explain why the quotient can be a whole number even if the dividend is fractional.

Assessment: source requires precise interpretation of unlabeled grid images, multiple possible unit conventions and grouping statements. A checked 18/135/50 alone cannot certify that a learner identified the correct whole and divisor-sized regions; teacher review of representations and explanations remains essential.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decimal dividend divided by one tenth
KeyConcepts.Definition: Count how many 0.1-sized pieces fit into the decimal amount.

KeyConcepts.Title: Divide by a hundredth
KeyConcepts.Definition: Count hundredths in the decimal total, including the whole part.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent rescaled quotients
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying both positive divisor and dividend by the same factor preserves quotient.
KeyConcepts.Example: The grid can describe both with properly labeled units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a large fractional dividend
WorkedExamples.Question: Find1.8÷0.1.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Interpret18 as a number of groups rather than a measure in whole units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Count hundredths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find1.35÷0.01.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two group sizes
WorkedExamples.Question: Find0.5÷0.1 and0.5÷0.01.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Write half a whole as five tenths or fifty hundredths.
Compare the two quotients and explain why the smaller group size yields more groups.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat dividing by0.01 as dividing by100
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 0.01 is a single hundredth and many such pieces fit into a whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count hundredth-sized pieces in the dividend rather than reducing it by a factor of100.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Read grid-cell counts without labeling the unit whole
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The same graphic might represent integer counts or fractional quantities depending on its declared whole.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explicitly label whether a large square is one or100 before comparing equations.

SummaryPoints: Decimal÷0.1 and decimal÷0.01 count fractional-sized groups.
An interpreted unit diagram can support equivalent decimal and whole-number division equations.
Source unit labeling and learner explanations require teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Book Drive (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: PLAN an original school book-sale fundraiser using purchase costs, marked-up selling prices, estimated quantities, decimal subtraction and multiplication, and a defensible range of possible profits. The source explicitly asks students to make assumptions about attendance and demand, not calculate one official profit amount. This optional activity has multiple valid plans.

Warm-up — pricing tradeoff: two fictional student groups buy a book for$7.25. Group A sells at$10.25, earning$3.00 per book. Group B sells at$11.50, earning$4.25. A higher sale price may bring higher profit PER BOOK but does not prove that more books will sell, because demand is uncertain. Do not claim a real sales forecast.

Activity 1 — compare the scenarios: if A sells36 books, it raises$108 in gross profit above purchase cost. If B sells24 books, it raises$102. If B instead sells24 books, A needs exactly34 sales to raise the same$102 because its profit is$3 per sale. Explain what data would actually be needed to predict which school sells more books.

Activity 2 — design an original fair: choose three categories from a fictional supply sheet: science books cost$8.40 and could sell for$11.40, storybooks cost$5.25 and could sell for$7.75, activity books cost$3.60 and could sell for$5.10. If a hypothetical school sells30,24 and40 of those, profit would be 30×$3=$90, 24×$2.50=$60, 40×$1.50=$60: $210 total. State that the number of copies sold, visitor choices and prices are assumptions, not actual market data. Develop too-low, plausible and too-high scenarios with different participation assumptions and explain the uncertainty.

Assessment: a class-designed book fair must include category choice, transparent costs and selling prices, assumptions about visitors/books purchased, multiple plausible totals and justifications. Teacher reviews financial modeling and ethics; neither the fixed$210 fictional example nor any numeric calculator should auto-mark the authentic planning task complete. No publisher price table or licensed illustrations reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Profit per book
KeyConcepts.Definition: Gross profit from one sale is selling price minus purchase cost, assuming no other expenses.
KeyConcepts.Example: The true net profit may also require other expenses not given.

KeyConcepts.Title: Total gross profit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Estimated category profit is per-book margin times an assumed number sold.
KeyConcepts.Example: Sum only compatible money values to get a modeled total.

KeyConcepts.Title: Models require demand assumptions
KeyConcepts.Definition: A higher mark-up may increase margin but may decrease quantity sold; no demand relationship is automatically given.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Profit=(price−cost)×quantity; the quantity itself is uncertain.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use low/base/high estimates and justify assumed participation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two prices
WorkedExamples.Question: A school pays$7.25 for a book; compare selling at$10.25 or$11.50.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Subtract purchase cost from each selling price.
Discuss why margin alone cannot predict demand.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher evaluates the explanation of price/attendance uncertainty.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match profits across groups
WorkedExamples.Question: Group B sells24 books at margin$4.25. How many sales at margin$3 would equal its gross profit?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: State the count with the assumption all sales have the same unit margin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plan a three-category example
WorkedExamples.Question: Find total hypothetical profit:30 science books at$3 margin,24 stories at$2.50,40 activities at$1.50.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party fraction-unit model with numeric inverse check. Student diagrams and modeling assumptions remain teacher-reviewed.
Steps: Multiply each count by its own margin.
Add for total, labeling the sales counts as invented planning assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer higher sale price guarantees higher total fundraiser profit
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of buyers can change when the price changes, and it is unknown in the scenario.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate unit profit from sales quantity and explicitly state demand assumptions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Label a fictional planning scenario as a real achieved fundraising result
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source is an estimation/modeling task, not a record of actual transactions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark estimates as conditional, record assumptions and ask a teacher to review the plan.

SummaryPoints: Book-sale profit models require cost, selling price, quantity and any extra expenses to be defined.
Different reasonable price/attendance assumptions lead to different valid totals.
The source's open modeling work cannot be automatically completed by one numeric answer.
